lines.n: The bed was soft enough to drown in. I lay on top of the covers in my traveling clothes and stared up at the pale blue hangings.
I lay down for an hour in the afternoon heat, like a lady. It didn't take.
I stretched out on the coverlet with my arms aching from the spade, and for once my head was quiet.
No. There was no time to lie down. Not now.
Fields and fields, and the blue smudge of a wood. Somewhere beyond them was the Wall, and beyond that, him.
A gardener was clipping the green flames along the drive, one careful snip at a time. Past the gates, the road ran west toward the old cottage.
The drive below was jammed with carts: crates of wine, gilt chairs, ladders, a whole wagon of flowers. Elain darted between them like a bee.
The lanterns from the ball still hung all down the drive, burnt out and turning in the wind. North was that way.
Right under the window lay Elain's garden: tulips in tidy rows, and Elain herself on her knees among them, a trowel in her fist.
Father's study, a footman told me, though nobody sat at the desk yet. Through the glass I could see a ledger, open, and a little brass scale.
Through the glass: stacks of ledgers, the brass scale, a velvet tray of stones. My fortune, written down in columns.

lines.t: Off for your walk? Take one of the footmen with you. No? Well. Mind the mud on the west road, then.

lines.n: Father had his nose an inch from a sapphire and didn't hear me come in. I left him to it.

lines.t: Well? Are you going to teach me, or stand there admiring the furniture?
If one more of them tells me my sister has gone very brown, I'll pour the punch down his breeches.

lines.n: My brushes, rinsed and laid out in a row. Nesta's paper was turned face down on the table. I didn't turn it over.
I picked up a brush, and put it down again. Not today.
The footman bowed so low I worried for his back.

lines.t: A fine morning for the garden, miss. Miss Elain's been out since dawn.

lines.n: He didn't quite manage to keep the horror off his face at the sight of a daughter of the house with a spade.

lines.t: Your horse is saddled, miss. Miss Elain saw to it herself.
Miss Elain's tulips, miss. Came across the sea in a crate, they did. We're not to lay a finger on them.

lines.n: Elain was on her knees among the tulips again, humming under her breath. I sat on the low wall and let her talk, and didn't hear half of it, and loved every word.

lines.t: Go. Please. Before Father comes down and makes this so much harder.

lines.n: Only trees. I didn't need to look again.
The fountain had been dry as long as I could remember. In summer the basin smelled of warm stone and pigeons.
Tomas and his friends had drifted off somewhere. It was only a dry basin again.
Still there. Cool and smooth as a pane of glass, and not a crack in it anywhere.
Cold ashes. I'd kicked earth over them myself.
